"We Shipped Everything and the Number Went Down"

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 24 September 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

The product is proven and the number still fell, so the problem has moved to distribution; stop building, name one story, and work one channel. Shipping more is rarely the fix. Pendo's analysis of 615 software products found 80% of features were rarely or never used, and at Microsoft only about a third of tested ideas improved the metric they targeted. Supply went up. Demand did not follow, because nobody was working demand.

What it usually means

The call comes after a big month of releases. The team moved fast. The core number (deposits, weekly active teams or paid seats) went down anyway.

Three things are usually true at once.

First, the product objection is dead. The thing works. It has worked for real users, repeatedly, across versions. Nobody who churned said it was broken.

Second, there is no lead story. The team has been telling three stories to three audiences. Each one is plausible. Together they cancel out. A buyer who hears three reasons to care hears none.

Third, shipping was the comfortable work. A release is visible, finite and hard to criticise. Distribution is slow, repetitive and easy to criticise. Given the choice, most teams build.

An onchain protocol launches a dozen new markets in a month and deposits fall. An AI product adds an integration every week while weekly active teams stay flat. The pattern is the same. Supply went up. Demand did not follow, because nobody was working demand.

This is a good month, even if it does not feel like one. It removes an explanation. The team can no longer say the product is not ready.

Why more releases do not move the number

The evidence on shipped features is consistent. Pendo, a product analytics vendor, aggregated three months of usage across 615 customer products in its 2019 Feature Adoption Report. About 12% of features generated 80% of daily usage, and 80% of features were rarely or never used. The sample is Pendo's own customers and the definition of a feature is a tagged part of an interface, so the exact figure is soft. The shape is not: most of what a team ships is not what users come for.

Controlled experiments say the same about ideas in general. Kohavi and Thomke reported in Harvard Business Review in 2017 that about a third of Microsoft's experiments improved their target metric, a third were neutral and a third made it worse. At Google and Bing the positive share was 10% to 20%. Those teams measure each change. A team that ships twelve unmeasured changes in a month has no way to know which of them hurt, and some probably did.

SignalWhat it suggests
Churned users say the product worksThe product objection is dead
Three audiences hear three storiesNo lead story; messages cancel out
Releases up, core number flat or downSupply added without demand work
New markets or integrations with no named partner behind themReleases went out into no channel
Number moves only when incentives runThe market will take it, not pay for it

Where it traces to

This traces to Part 1 and Part 8.

Part 1 asked for one system, not three problems. One named buyer, one calendar, one owner. A team running three stories has skipped this. The shipping cadence filled the gap where the buyer definition should have been.

Part 8 covered distribution when platforms are closed. The channel sort (open, restricted, closed) was meant to be done before the roadmap was set. If it was never done, releases went out into no channel at all.

In crypto this also traces to Parts 19 and 20. New markets without issuers, integrations and curators lined up are supply with no demand. Protocol revenue does not follow from more venues. It follows from the venues that already have the depositor.

In AI it traces to Part 13. A shallow integration is not distribution. The partner who already has the team is.

The first move this week

Stop building for sixty days. Fixes and security work continue. New features do not. Put it in writing so the team knows it is a decision, not a mood.

Name one lead story. Not the best one, the one you can prove. Write it in a sentence a partner could repeat without you in the room.

Pick one channel band and work it exclusively. For most teams at this point it is partners who already have your buyer. They have the trust and the list. You have the product that works. The scale of that route is large: Canalys, an industry analyst, forecast that partners would deliver 70% of the $5.44 trillion spent on IT worldwide in 2025. Partner channel design covers how to set the partner's role and economics before recruiting, and ecosystem-led growth covers using partner customer overlap to pick the twenty. Make a list of twenty, contact all of them, and run it like Part 4 said to run a round.

The market did not change in the month you shipped twelve things. Your attention did.

Report the number two ways

Report the core number two ways from this week on.

LineWhat it shows
With incentives and free tierWhat the market will take when paid to take it
Without incentives and free tierWhat the market will pay for

If the second line is flat while the first moves, you have been buying the number. Now everyone can see it.

The split matters because incentive effects are often temporary and hard to read without a comparison. Gauntlet, a risk-modelling firm, analysed Uniswap's liquidity-mining programme for the protocol's governance forum in June 2023, comparing incentivised pools with control pools. Results were mixed: some pools settled at a higher level after rewards stopped, one large spike in deposits disappeared, and two pools showed no statistically significant lift. Without the control pools and the post-programme read, the lasting effect could not have been separated from the paid one. The same logic applies to a free tier in a product-led motion: free usage shows reach, paid conversion shows demand.

What not to do

Do not ship one more feature. The next one will not be the one.

Do not announce more partnerships. A logo on a slide is not a partner working your buyer.

Do not blame the market. The market did not change in the month you shipped twelve things. Your attention did.

How you know it worked

Two signs. The core number without incentives moves up, even slightly, within the sixty days. And at least one partner is bringing buyers without being chased each week.

Illustrative example: sixty days without a release
Decision
Freeze new features for sixty days, lead with one story about settlement speed, and work twenty payment partners who already served the target merchants.
Reason and owner
Eleven releases in a quarter had coincided with a fall in paying accounts, and churned users cited price and fit, not defects. Owned by the CEO, with the head of partnerships running the list.
What changed
Three partners began referring merchants without prompting by week seven. Paying accounts without incentives rose slightly while the incentivised total was flat, which showed the earlier growth had been bought.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage fintech infrastructure company, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Read the falling number as a distribution signal. If the product works and the number fell, building more will not fix it.
  • Most shipped features go unused. Supply without a lead story and a channel adds cost, not demand.
  • Freeze, name, work. Sixty days without new features, one provable story, one channel band and a list of twenty.
  • Split the number. With and without incentives, every week, so nobody mistakes bought growth for demand.
Gateway card

Before the next release ships

  • A written sixty-day build freeze, with the exceptions named
  • One lead story in one sentence, and one channel band with a list of twenty
  • The core number reported with and without incentives, every week
  • A named partner who will carry the release to buyers

Common questions

Why did our metrics drop after a big product release?

Usually because the product works but there is no single lead story and nobody was working demand. Supply went up and demand did not follow. Most features also go unused, so more of them rarely moves the core number.

What should a startup do when shipping more features doesn't grow usage?

Stop building new features for sixty days, name one lead story you can prove, and work one channel band, often partners who already have your buyer, starting with a list of twenty.

How can I tell if incentives are inflating my growth numbers?

Report the core number with and without incentives and free tier. If the second line is flat while the first moves, you have been buying the number.

What percentage of software features are actually used?

In Pendo's 2019 vendor analysis of 615 products, about 80% of features were rarely or never used, and roughly 12% of features generated 80% of daily usage.

Sources and notes

  • Pendo, The 2019 Feature Adoption Report, 2019. Vendor analysis of 615 of its own customers' products over three months; "feature" is Pendo's tagging unit.
  • Kohavi and Thomke, The surprising power of online experiments, Harvard Business Review, September to October 2017. Large technology firms; hosted copy.
  • Canalys, IT spending forecasts 2025, November 2024. Analyst forecast of partner-delivered share; covers IT broadly, not crypto or early-stage AI.
  • Gauntlet, Uniswap liquidity mining analysis, 6 June 2023. Paid risk consultant to the protocol; five pools, post-programme data one week after rewards ended.
  • The signal table, two-line report and example are lowob's framework and illustration.
